title: Berk v. Choy (2026)
summary: When a valid Federal Rule of Civil Procedure answers the question in dispute, it displaces a conflicting state law in federal court, so Delaware's affidavit-of-merit requirement for malpractice suits gives way to Rule 8 without any Erie analysis.
notes: U.S. Supreme Court, 2026. Key line: "Thus, a valid Rule of Civil Procedure displaces contrary state law even if the state law would qualify as substantive under Erie's test." (Justice Barrett, for the Court)

sections.Parties: Petitioner Harold R. Berk was an out-of-state visitor who was injured in Delaware and became the plaintiff in a medical malpractice suit. He sued in federal court because he and the defendants were citizens of different States, which gave the district court diversity jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. 1332. Respondents were Dr. Wilson C. Choy, the physician who treated Berk's ankle, and Beebe Medical Center, Inc., the corporation that owned the hospital where he was treated. The opinion calls Choy and Beebe together the defendants. Both defendants defended the suit on the ground that Berk had not filed the affidavit of merit that Delaware law demands, and both argued in the Supreme Court that the Delaware statute should be enforced in federal court.
sections.Material Facts: While on a trip to Delaware, Berk fell out of bed. An ambulance took him to a Beebe hospital, where an X ray showed a fractured ankle. Dr. Choy recommended a protective boot. Hospital employees forced Berk's leg into the boot and twisted the fractured ankle. Choy did not order another X ray at once; he told Berk to keep weight off the ankle and set a follow-up in two weeks. The second X ray showed an ankle that was severely deformed, and surgery was required. Delaware law, Del. Code Tit. 18, section 6853, says no health-care negligence suit may be filed unless an affidavit of merit signed by a medical professional accompanies the complaint. A plaintiff with good cause may get one 60-day extension, but must move for it with or before the complaint. Otherwise the clerk must refuse to docket the complaint, and defendants need not respond until 20 days after the affidavit is filed.
sections.Procedural History: Berk sued Choy and Beebe for malpractice under Delaware law in the District of Delaware. He moved at once for an extension to file an affidavit and the court granted it, but he could not find a doctor willing to sign one, so he filed his medical records under seal instead. Defendants moved for in camera review of those submissions under section 6853. Berk answered that the statute could not be enforced in federal court because the Federal Rules displaced it. The District Court disagreed and dismissed the suit in April 2023. The Third Circuit affirmed in July 2024. It held that the Federal Rules were silent on whether an affidavit must accompany a complaint, applied the Hanna outcome-determination and twin-aims test, found section 6853 substantive, and upheld the dismissal. The Supreme Court granted certiorari, heard argument on October 6, 2025, and decided the case on January 20, 2026, reversing and remanding.
sections.Issue: Does Delaware's affidavit-of-merit statute apply to a state-law medical malpractice claim brought in federal court under diversity jurisdiction, or does a Federal Rule of Civil Procedure answer the same question and displace the state requirement? Put in the framework of Hanna and Shady Grove, the question has two parts. First, does any Federal Rule answer the disputed question, which the majority frames as whether Berk's suit may be dismissed because his complaint was not accompanied by an expert affidavit? Second, if a Rule does answer that question, is the Rule valid under the Rules Enabling Act, 28 U.S.C. 2072(b), which forbids rules that abridge, enlarge or modify a substantive right? A further contested point is whether the validity inquiry also asks whether the displaced state law is substantive.
sections.Holding: Delaware's affidavit law does not apply in federal court. Rule 8 answers the disputed question. By requiring only a short and plain statement of the claim, Rule 8 sets a ceiling on the information a plaintiff can be required to supply about the merits at the outset, and Rule 12 confirms that a court may not look beyond the pleadings when deciding whether a claim has been stated. Section 6853 demands evidence as well as allegations, so the two give different answers. Rule 8 is valid under the Rules Enabling Act because it really regulates procedure, and the substantive nature or purpose of the displaced state law makes no difference to that validity question. The judgment of the Third Circuit was reversed and the case remanded. Justice Barrett wrote for eight Justices; Justice Jackson concurred only in the judgment.
sections.Reasoning: The Rules of Decision Act sends federal courts to state substantive law unless a federal statute otherwise provides, and the Rules Enabling Act is such a statute. So when a Federal Rule is on point, the court bypasses Erie's murky waters and asks only whether the Rule answers the question in dispute, and whether the Rule is within the Enabling Act. Rule 8(a)(2) requires a short and plain statement showing entitlement to relief, which establishes, implicitly but with unmistakable clarity, that evidence is not required. Rule 12(b)(6) supplies the only merits ground for dismissal, Rule 12(d) bars matters outside the pleadings, and Twombly asks only whether the allegations are plausible. Leatherman and Jones v. Bock rejected efforts to demand more. Cohen did not exempt state preconditions to proceeding; it found no conflict because the bond statute and old Rule 23 addressed different issues. Defendants' proposal to enforce the affidavit later in the case rewrites the statute, and no Federal Rule would enforce it anyway; Rule 56 is the mechanism for putting a plaintiff to his proof, and it requires time for discovery. Rule 11(a)'s proviso covers verification by parties, not affidavits from third parties. Under Sibbach, a Rule is valid if it really regulates procedure, and Rule 8 governs only the manner and means of enforcing rights.

topics.cp-rule-scope: The first question is whether a Federal Rule, read by its plain meaning, answers the question in dispute; here Rule 8 and section 6853 both address what a plaintiff must supply about the merits at the outset.
topics.cp-rules-enabling: A Rule that answers the question governs if it really regulates procedure under Sibbach, and the substantive nature or purpose of the displaced state law makes no difference to that inquiry.
topics.cp-erie: When a valid Federal Rule is on point the court bypasses Erie entirely, so the Third Circuit erred by running the Hanna outcome and twin-aims test on the Delaware statute.
topics.cp-frcp-8: Rule 8(a)(2)'s short and plain statement is a ceiling on merits information as well as a floor, so a state cannot require evidence such as an expert affidavit to accompany the complaint.
topics.cp-frcp-12: Rule 12(b)(6) is the only merits ground for dismissal and Rule 12(d) bars matters outside the pleadings, which reinforces the conflict and, for Justice Jackson, supplies it.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Jackson concurred in the judgment. She agreed that the Delaware requirement cannot apply in federal court but located the conflict in Rules 3 and 12 rather than Rule 8. In her view the question section 6853 answers is what is required to start a malpractice action; Rule 3 answers that a civil action is commenced by filing a complaint, period, so the two collide. Rule 8, by its terms, governs only what a pleading must contain, and the majority conceded the affidavit is not a pleading, so stretching Rule 8 to cover a separate document is a contortion. She also relied on Gasperini for the view that Federal Rules must be read with sensitivity to state interests, and she distinguished Walker and Woods. She found the Rule 12(d) conflict sufficient by itself, because the Delaware Supreme Court reads section 6853 as a ground for dismissal, and she faulted the majority for treating the affidavit as outside the pleadings for Rule 12 and inside them for Rule 8. The majority answered in footnotes that Berk's suit had already been docketed, that negative inferences from text are legitimate, and that the concurrence's Rule 3 argument depends on the same kind of inference.
learning.why: Berk is the newest step on the Hanna and Shady Grove track: when a Federal Rule answers the disputed question, the court never reaches Erie's twin aims, and the Rule survives the Rules Enabling Act if it really regulates procedure, no matter how substantive the state law looks. It also treats Rule 8 as a ceiling as well as a floor, which matters for every state screening device aimed at federal diversity plaintiffs.

mnemonic.rationale: An affidavit of merit that Rule 8 displaced
